cards.title: Connect unrelated premiums to your product with a logical bridge
cards.summary: Even a premium that seems unrelated to your product can work if the copy connects it to the product's USP through a logical comparison.
cards.use_when: Choosing a premium for a subscription, membership or information product where the obvious physical premium seems off-category.
steps: Identify the premium's core function and the product's core function, then find the distinction that makes the product superior (speed vs. depth, headline vs. detail, summary vs. analysis).
Write copy that first credits the premium with its genuine strength, then pivots to why the product is the better or more complete resource.
Example from the source: Newsweek offered a free AM/FM radio. Milt Pierce's letter said the radio is the fastest way to get the news, but Newsweek is the best way to get news in depth.
For a Swiss-bank-account-branded investment newsletter, a free Swiss bank account premium dramatized the USP of offshore investing and privacy.
caveats: The bridge must be honest: the premium's strength is stated first, not dismissed.
This works best when the premium is thematically adjacent to the buyer's aspiration, not merely expensive.

cards.title: Reduce friction to accept: multiple response channels and minimal form fields
cards.summary: Offer every plausible way to respond and ask for the fewest fields possible, because each forced field incrementally reduces conversion.
cards.use_when: Designing order forms, lead capture pages, direct-mail reply devices or opt-in flows.
steps: Offer multiple response mechanisms: toll-free phone, fax, landing page link, email and postal address. Different prospects respond different ways.
In direct mail, enclose a fax-back form or business reply card with the sales letter; add a business reply envelope if you want payment enclosed or privacy matters.
In print, include a coupon or a bind-in BRC opposite the ad.
On the web, ask for the minimum: for opt-in list building, name and email only.
When multiple fields exist, mark mandatory fields with an asterisk and make as many fields optional as possible. Conversion declines with each additional required field.
Turn the reply mechanism into a stated benefit where possible. Sig Rosenblum's Board Report letter said the card was already addressed and postage was paid.
caveats: The source states conversion declines incrementally per forced field but gives no specific numeric rate for ecommerce checkout; treat it as direction, not a benchmark.
Payment-required purchases will inherently need more fields than pure lead capture.

cards.title: Remove risk and obligation to lower sales pressure
cards.summary: Explicitly state that the prospect faces no sales visit, no call and no obligation, and use the word 'free' rather than 'complimentary'.
cards.use_when: Writing offer copy for lead magnets, whitepapers, webinars, trials or any offer where prospects fear being pursued by sales.
steps: If leads are followed up by phone rather than field sales, say 'No salesperson will visit' in the copy.
If leads are not followed up by phone, say 'No salesperson will call.'

When something is free, call it free. Do not substitute 'complimentary' for a high-level business audience out of fear 'free' sounds unprofessional — the source argues it does not offend and everyone wants free things.
State that no further action is required after acceptance: 'There's no obligation … nothing to buy … and no commitment of any kind.'
caveats: The A/B test cited (a free pocket diary lifting doctor symposium attendance six-fold) is a single example, not a guaranteed multiplier for ecommerce.
Only claim 'no salesperson will call' if that is operationally true; false claims create support and trust problems.

cards.title: Use multiple premiums and value them credibly
cards.summary: Two premiums are often better than one, especially for information buyers, and assigning a real, demonstrable dollar value to each premium increases believability.
cards.use_when: Building a stacked offer for a subscription, course, book or product bundle.
steps: Consider offering two or more premiums; Dick Benson's Secrets of Successful Direct Mail states two premiums are frequently better than one, and information-product buyers especially like multiple premiums.

For digital premiums (PDFs, downloadable reports), delivery cost is near zero, so the number can be large. The source cites a book promotion with roughly a dozen free special reports that reached #1 nonfiction on Amazon with 900+ orders in a day.
Assign a dollar value by printing a price in the upper right corner of the report cover.
Prove the price is real by selling the same reports in a cart on your main site at that price; then you can honestly say 'we actually sell this report at this price on our website.'
Michael Bell of Phillips Publishing suggests the combined stated value of the premiums should exceed the subscription price so the buyer gets their money's worth from premiums alone.
caveats: The Amazon result is a case example, not a promised outcome.
Inflated valuations without a real cart price undermine the credibility the technique depends on.

cards.title: Premiums as first-purchase and continuity incentives
cards.summary: Premiums can be structured to trigger first purchase or to keep customers buying through a series.
cards.use_when: Designing continuity programs, subscription boxes, collectible series or first-order incentives.
steps: Use a first-order premium to convert new customers. Gevalia offered a free 12-cup coffeemaker with the first order of a monthly gourmet coffee subscription.
Use a completion premium to drive series collection. Franklin Mint's Civil War chess set shipped one piece per month; after all 32 pieces were purchased, the customer received a free chessboard.
For ecommerce, the equivalent is a bonus item unlocked at a purchase threshold or after a set number of reorders.
caveats: Completion premiums create a long commitment and require inventory planning for the eventual free item.
The source presents these as examples of incentive design, not tested uplift figures.

cards.title: Benson's rules of thumb for offer mechanics
cards.summary: A set of direct-marketing rules of thumb from Dick Benson covering sweepstakes, bill-me terms, memberships, installments and premium-versus-discount choices.
cards.use_when: Choosing which offer mechanism to test first, or sizing the expected direction of an offer test.
steps: These are the source's reported rules of thumb from Benson's Secrets of Successful Direct Mail:
Sweepstakes improve results by 50 percent or more.
A credit or bill-me offer improves results by 50 percent or more.
Memberships renew better than plain subscriptions by 10 percent or more.
Adding installment payments for items over $15 increases results by 15 percent.
If you must choose one, premiums work better than cash discounts.
Subscriptions sold at half price for at least eight months convert at renewal just as strongly as full-price annual subscriptions.
Offering a choice of terms (one year vs. two years) pulls more gross dollars but about 10 percent fewer subscriptions.
Offering an incentive to pay cash when both cash and credit are offered reduces net response.
caveats: These are general direct-marketing heuristics from a 1992 book, not verified benchmarks for modern ecommerce. Treat them as test hypotheses.
Sweepstakes and bill-me terms may attract lower-quality buyers; measure downstream value, not just response.

cards.title: Price can be raised to increase sales when the price signals quality
cards.summary: A price that is too low for a professional audience can signal 'not a serious tool', while doubling the price can increase sales with that audience.
cards.use_when: Repositioning a product toward a professional or higher-intent segment, or when low-price positioning has stalled.
steps: Recognize that pricing is often counterintuitive: the price you assume sells best frequently does not.
Example from the source: a software company priced at $79 per desktop to appeal to both consumers and professionals; consumers found it too high and professionals read it as not serious.
They refocused on the professional market and raised the price to $129. Sales soared.
Test price points as part of the offer rather than assuming lower is always better.
caveats: This result came from a deliberate segment shift, not a pure price test on the same audience. Raising price without changing positioning or audience may not reproduce it.
The source names price as probably the most important component to test, alongside payment terms, premium and guarantee.

cards.title: State discounts as dollar amounts, not percentages, when the value is fixed
cards.summary: When a discount has a fixed dollar value, lead with the dollar figure, which generated nearly three times the revenue of the equivalent percentage in an email test.
cards.use_when: Writing coupon, sale or email subject-line copy where the savings amount is the same regardless of format.
steps: Test '$50-off coupon' against '15%-off coupon' where both equal a $50 discount. The source reports the $50-off version generated nearly three times more revenue.

Use percentage framing where the discount is inherently a fixed percentage and the dollar value varies by product, model or option selected. Geico's '15 minutes could save you 15 percent' is the cited percentage example.
Choose the framing that puts the more concrete number in front of the buyer.
caveats: The nearly-3x result is from one cited test reported in The Marketing Report (9/8/08); treat as a hypothesis to test in your own list.
Both framings can work; the rule is about which number is fixed and which is variable.

cards.title: Make an expensive price feel smaller: per-day math
cards.summary: Divide the total price by the days or period of use to state a much smaller daily figure in the copy.
cards.use_when: Selling annual subscriptions, memberships or high-ticket items where the lump sum causes resistance.
steps: Divide the total price by the length of service. Example: Georgia Publishing's American Speaker at $297 for a year's subscription becomes 'just 81 cents a day.'
An options trading course at $29.95/month can be stated as 'less than a dollar a day.'
An annual subscription at $197 becomes '54 cents a day.'

Warning from the source: divide by length of service or subscription, but avoid price-per-book or price-per-page comparisons, because specialized information always looks expensive per page next to trade books and periodicals.
caveats: This is a framing device, not a change to actual payment terms. If the buyer must pay the full sum up front, the copy should still be clear about that.

cards.title: Compare price against other categories addressing the same need
cards.summary: Anchor your price against more expensive alternatives in other categories that satisfy the same underlying need.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy for products with higher-priced substitutes or do-it-yourself alternatives (ecommerce, courses, tools, services).
steps: Identify what the buyer would otherwise spend to solve the same problem, including services a professional would charge for.

The source's examples: an ab machine compared to 'thousands on an expensive gym membership', priced at three payments of $19.95; a newsletter with the same stock recommendations that private clients pay $2,000 a year for.
Talk about the higher-priced options and alternatives first, so the actual price lands as a relief.
Cialdini's retail example: placing even more expensive sweaters at the store entrance made the intended line feel like a bargain by the time customers reached it.
caveats: Comparisons must be defensible; the source explicitly endorses apples-to-oranges comparisons against consultation or training, but the comparison still has to be honest to hold up.
Do not invent competitor prices or service costs.

cards.title: Exploit the first-payment effect with installments and low-entry trials
cards.summary: Buyers psychologically react to the first payment and discount future payments, so a higher total split into installments can outsell a lower lump sum.
cards.use_when: Setting payment terms for courses, subscriptions, software and higher-priced products.
steps: Design offers so the first payment is the small, decision-relevant number.
A/B test cited: $49 for one year vs. four quarterly payments of $39 (= $156/year). The $156 offer won, more than tripling the stated cost, because prospects mentally compared $49 to $39.

A $1 14-day trial can be used to capture card details: the source describes an options course at $29.95/month that added a $1 14-day trial with cancellation and refund available, which significantly increased sales. The $1 existed to get the card submitted, not to process revenue.
Rodale's book offers, e.g. three payments of $9.95 for a roughly $30 book, rely on the buyer hearing '$9.95', not '$30'.

Rich Schefren's Strategic Profits waits until month three to offer an upsell, because cancellation likelihood drops sharply after month three, and appends the upsell's payments to the end of the schedule rather than charging immediately.
caveats: The source advises running all promotional copy, especially time-limited offers, past an attorney; installment and trial terms have regulatory implications.
This relies on the buyer's tendency to discount future payments. It can attract buyers who later churn; measure total collected, not first-payment conversions.

cards.title: The magic of a dollar and the magic of a penny
cards.summary: 'Free' is powerful but a dollar-and-a-penny offer is nearly as powerful, because it changes the framing and sometimes enables a physical gimmick.
cards.use_when: Packaging a paid offer so it can be advertised at a near-zero entry price.
steps: Consider whether part of the offer can be split so a component is advertised at one dollar or one penny while the essential component carries the real price.

Example: an integrated accounting suite at $249 was split into modules at $1 each plus a $244 general ledger that every module required. The 'accounting software for a dollar' mailing generated 10 times more orders than the 'integrated accounting software for $249' control.

A commercial cleaning company was advised to charge one penny instead of cleaning for free, so it could spot-glue a penny to the top of the sales letter: 'We will clean your offices or plant for only a penny … and we've even enclosed the penny to get you started!'
caveats: The source describes this as a gimmick that worked; the 10x result is one company's control comparison.
The penny/spot-glue tactic is direct mail specific. The transferable idea for ecommerce is splitting a price so a component can honestly be advertised at $1.

cards.title: Drop-in-the-bucket technique to preempt sticker shock
cards.summary: Build the perception of value and compare the price to larger alternatives before stating it, so the actual figure lands as a drop in the bucket.
cards.use_when: Writing a sales page for a product priced above the obvious reference category, including e-books and information products.
steps: Explain what the product actually is and where its value comes from before revealing price; reframe it away from the cheap comparison category.
Compare the price to the cost of hiring the author or expert. The source's example: a $79 e-book compared to 'well over $25,000' of accumulated work and 'about $200 an hour' for a lawyer.
Stack descending numbers so the final price feels small: 'won't cost you $25,000 … or $1,000 … or even $200. Instead, the price is just $79.'
Add delivery and access benefits in the same breath (immediate download, no shipping, no waiting).

Mike Pavlish's framing: convince the prospect the price is a drop in the bucket compared to the value received, and do it before you give the price. The source says it uses this for every offer, not just high-priced ones.
caveats: Values cited in the copy must be traceable to something real (the author's rates, the price of alternatives), or the anchor collapses under scrutiny.
For ecommerce, translate the anchor into real substitute costs: assembly, installation, professional service, or replacing the item later.

cards.title: Twelve ways to overcome sticker shock
cards.summary: A checklist of tactics beyond drop-in-the-bucket for making a high price acceptable.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a high-priced sales page or offer where the price is revealed and resistance is expected.
steps: 1. Compare the product's cost to the cost of hiring the author (the source cites $500/hour, so an e-book costs 'less than five minutes of my time').
2. Make the prospect relieved to hear your price by stating higher prices for other options first (laser eye surgery $1,000, optician glasses $300, your specs $19.95).
3. Make apples-to-oranges comparisons against other information resources, not direct competitors (a $297 subscription vs. $5,000 for one speech from a top speechwriter).
4. Spread out payments; 'till forbid' monthly credit card billing is one form.
5. State the price in the smallest true terms, e.g. per day.
6. Value the component parts and show their retail sum exceeds the bundle price.
7. Add an element the buyer cannot easily price, like a CD-ROM with a loose-leaf service, to break direct comparison.
8. Use a calculator to dramatize compounding outcomes.
9. Pre-empt the objection by stating the high price up front and using it to exclude non-prospects.
10. Use a false close: bring the prospect to the point of ordering, then add another benefit before asking for the order.
11. Add a sweetener: extra premium, extended guarantee, free support, or two-for-one.
12. Establish yourself as the leading expert in your niche; price resistance diminishes with perceived authority.
caveats: Several of these tactics are framing devices; the underlying price and value must still be real to avoid refunds and reputation damage.

The compounding-math example ('5 percent monthly for 10 years turns $10,000 into $3.4 million') is an illustrative dramatization, not a forecast. Do not present hypothetical returns as likely outcomes.

cards.title: Good-better-best pricing to raise average order value
cards.summary: Offer three tiers and expect the middle to win, while the low and free tiers defuse 'too expensive' objections and feed a funnel.
cards.use_when: Structuring product tiers, coaching/service ladders or supplement-style bundles.
steps: Build a ladder from free content, to a $10–50 book/e-book, to a $100–300 self-study package, to mid-range coaching with some personal contact, to high-touch premium consulting priced in the thousands.

For physical products, the equivalent three options are: a large supply at a discount with free premiums and free shipping (best value), a mid-size supply with one bonus and free shipping, and a single unit with no premiums and paid shipping.
Expect the majority to take the middle option; the cheapest feels insufficient and the most expensive feels excessive.
The presence of the low-priced and free options makes it hard for prospects to accuse you of being overpriced, since you can point them to the cheaper ways to access your knowledge.
Use the ladder as a sales funnel to move buyers up to higher packages over time.
caveats: The source states the middle-option preference as a rule that holds with almost every product, but gives no measured conversion split.
Tier design must keep the middle option genuinely adequate; a deliberately crippled middle tier damages trust.

cards.title: The four guarantee decisions: length, conditionality, coverage, activation
cards.summary: A guarantee has four design levers, and longer plus unconditional generally lifts response while conditions and ambiguity suppress it.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising a guarantee for any product, especially high-priced or downloadable ones.
steps: Length: the minimum used in direct marketing is 10 days; a two-week guarantee is common for trading services so the window closes before buyer's remorse; 30 days is the most common; the source prefers 60 or 90 days. Lifetime guarantees are not recommended for solo entrepreneurs because they leave a permanent liability, and dated information products shouldn't carry long guarantees.

Conditionality: avoid conditional guarantees such as 'in saleable condition' or 'show a sincere effort'. Buyers fear the seller will claim they used the materials wrong and refuse the refund. The unconditional guarantee works best and should be stated as such: 'no questions asked.'

Coverage: decide whether shipping and handling is refunded. If it is not, say 'product refund' rather than 'full refund'. The source does not refund shipping and handling; some sellers go further and pay return shipping.
Activation: the clock should run from receipt of goods, not order date, and the copy should spell out exactly how to get a refund (e.g. return the unused portion, or even the empty bottles).
caveats: Double-your-money-back guarantees can be powerful; the source cites a doctors' oral board workshop where adding it tripled attendance and revenue. That is an example, not a benchmark.
The source is explicit that it is not giving legal advice; consult an attorney on guarantee terms and any persistent-customer disputes.
Directories should not get long guarantees, because a buyer could use the edition for a year and then return it.

cards.title: Make the guarantee visually prominent
cards.summary: A guarantee buried in small print does not do its job; set it in larger type inside a bordered or certificate-style block.
cards.use_when: Laying out a sales page, direct-mail piece or product page that contains a guarantee.
steps: Give the guarantee its own headline in large bold type.
Set the guarantee body copy around 12-point type.
Put a box or certificate-style border around the guarantee block.
Do not hide the guarantee in body copy or an asterisked footnote in 8-point type.

Write the terms clearly to avoid misinterpretation. Example rewrite from the source: instead of a performance-only condition, say 'If you do not make extra money trading options with our program, or you are not 100 percent satisfied for any other reason — or for no reason — just return the program within 90 days for a full refund.'
caveats: Prominence only helps if the terms are simple; a visually bold but conditional guarantee still raises suspicion.

cards.title: Unfair advantage offer for digital products
cards.summary: For downloadable products the buyer cannot return, let them keep the file with a refund, trading a small amount of abuse for a large lift in conversion.
cards.use_when: Selling e-books, PDF courses, templates or other non-returnable digital downloads.
steps: State the guarantee so the buyer keeps the product after a refund: 'I'll send you a prompt refund … and you can still keep the e-book with my compliments.'
Actively surface the buyer's ability to take advantage, e.g. that they may use a software tool during the 30-day window, recode their systems, and still return it.
The source's e-book refund rate is described as a tiny fraction of 1 percent, and conversion rose after adding the copy.
David Powers tested telling buyers they could keep the e-book either way and reported a 21 percent increase in conversion and sales.
For the Y2K software case cited, explicitly offering the use-then-return path was very profitable and returns were no higher than normal.
caveats: The 21 percent figure is one marketer's test result, not a promise.
Requiring deletion of a downloaded file is unenforceable, so the source does not require it.
Works because most buyers are honest; monitor actual refund rates before rolling out broadly.

cards.title: Use deadlines to force an act-now decision
cards.summary: Time limits are the simplest urgency mechanism; choose a specific date only if you control timing, otherwise use a generic response window.
cards.use_when: Adding urgency to a promotion, email, landing page or direct-mail piece.
steps: Pick one of two formats: a specific date ('Offer expires March 15, 2009') or a generic window ('You must reply within 15 days').

Use a specific date only if printing and mailing timing is under control, so the piece does not arrive after the date. If you print in large quantities or mail continuously, use the generic window so it works whenever the piece lands.

Set length by channel: for direct mail, 15–21 days is reasonable. For email, shorter windows work ('this week only', 'expires in 48 hours'), and one or two follow-up reminder emails near the deadline generate additional orders.
On a landing page, display a real-time clock or counter of days or hours remaining.
For consumer direct mail, a 7-, 11- or 15-day reply window with a quick-response bonus (a free report for replying within seven days) is common.
Infomercials compress this further: eliminate one installment for callers within 20–30 minutes, equivalent to a 25 percent discount.
caveats: The source explicitly advises running promotional copy past an attorney, especially time-limited offers: once you state an expiry date, you generally cannot extend it.
A deadline that is not enforced trains the audience to ignore future deadlines.

cards.title: Trial length: test 30 vs. 60 vs. 90 days and the word 'trial' vs. 'use'
cards.summary: A longer trial can lift response until it hits a ceiling, and replacing 'trial' with 'use' can lift it further when the word 'trial' carries negative work connotations.
cards.use_when: Designing free-trial or free-use offers for software or products that require setup/learning effort.
steps: Test trial length against your standard. In the source's mainframe software case, 60 days outperformed the standard 30 days by 10 percent; 90 days produced no further lift over 60.

Diagnose why the standard length fails. The source's conclusion: 30 days was not enough for a busy IT professional to install and test software, so prospects returned it feeling the window was expiring before they had tested it.

Then test the label. In the same company's mailing, '60-day free use' outperformed '60-day free trial' by 15 percent, because 'trial' connoted broken batch files and weekend testing, while 'use' felt positive.
Apply the same logic to ecommerce: give enough time for the product to be actually used before the billing decision, and name the offer after the benefit rather than the risk.
caveats: Both results are single-company split tests; the direction is a hypothesis for your audience.
Longer trials delay cash collection and increase the window for cancellation.

cards.title: Limit quantity or enrollment with a credible reason
cards.summary: Scarcity via limited quantity, limited seats or limited membership works best when the limitation is specific, credible and true.
cards.use_when: Promoting events, cohorts, capacity-constrained services or launches where supply or capacity is genuinely finite.
steps: Use the limited-number framing: 'This offer is limited to the first 200 people who respond.' The source notes this works because recipients don't know how many were mailed.

Give a legitimate reason for the limit. Examples: prototyping capacity constrained by staff ('If you are not one of the first to respond, you may well have to wait longer than we'd both like'); a $1,500 advisory service capped at 1,000 subscribers because the publisher could not otherwise ensure good trade execution, with copy stating checks would be returned uncashed past the cap.
For events, seminars and workshops, state that limited seats are first-come, first-served.
A scarcity line can be literally true and still convey limited supply, e.g. Bill Jayme's 'Only so many copies of the premiere issue will be printed — no more.'
Use early-bird discounts for events and pre-publication offers: a $500 discount on a $2,497 seminar; even $5–10 off a $100 book or directory can lift response.
caveats: The source warns not to sacrifice credibility. A 'we printed only 1,000 copies' claim fails when the premium is a downloadable PDF or MP3, since the company could obviously print more.
Invented limits can work, but the source advises respecting the prospect's intelligence; a transparently fake cap destroys the tactic.

cards.title: Choose premiums differently for lead generation than for sales
cards.summary: For sales, premium desirability matters most (Benson); for lead generation the source favors premiums related to the product to avoid unqualified freebie seekers.
cards.use_when: Selecting a premium for a purchase offer versus a lead magnet for opt-ins or B2B inquiries.
steps: Per Dick Benson, the primary criteria for premium selection are perceived value and desirability; relevance to the product is secondary. Benson's view is that a premium need not relate to the product.

The source partly disagrees: in lead generation, a desirable premium matters, but the source puts more weight on a premium related to the product, because unrelated high-value premiums bring in freebie seekers and unqualified leads.

For B2B and corporate buyers, be aware that some organizations forbid employees from accepting vendor gifts (defense contractors are cited). A mail test of a 25 percent discount versus the same discount plus a free clock radio found the premium depressed response. Possible reason given: buyers feared being seen as accepting a bribe, or assumed the price included the gift's cost.

If you offer a B2B premium, consider making it relevant to the buyer's company rather than personal, so the buyer looks like a sharp purchaser. The cited example: a free CD-ROM stacker/reader offered with a group of high-priced CD-ROM information products.
caveats: The depressed-response test is described as business-gift-specific; do not generalize it to consumer ecommerce without testing.
The source presents the Benson disagreement explicitly, so this is a situational choice, not a single rule.

Even when the offer does not at first glance seem closely related to the product, a clever copywriter can find a connection. Example: Years ago, Newsweek offered a free radio as a premium for new subscribers. It would seem that a radio was a poor choice for a premium: In the news area, radio and magazines compete with one another. But copywriter Milt Pierce used the differences between these media to make a logical connection between the premium and the product: Dear Reader: What’s the fastest way to get the news? It’s on the radio. That’s why Newsweek wants you to have — as an introductory gift for new subscribers — this superb AM/FM radio. But what’s the best way to get the news? You won’t get just headlines and a rough outline of the news, with Newsweek; you’ll get the news in depth … 5. Easy to take advantage of. You should make it as easy and convenient as possible for the prospect to accept your offer.

 How? To begin with, offer multiple response mechanisms: toll-free phone number … fax number … a hyperlink to a landing page (see www.thelandingpageguru.com) … e-mail … even (gasp!) a postal address. Different prospects respond in different ways. In a direct-mail package, enclose a fax-back form or business reply card (BRC) with your sales letter. If you want customers to enclose payment with their order, or privacy is a concern, also include a business reply envelope (BRE). In a print ad, consider including a coupon or a bind-in BRC opposite the advertisement. On the Web, your landing page should ask for the minimum information from the prospect when collecting leads. If you are building your opt-in e-list, ask for name and e-mail address only. When you have multiple fields for the user to complete, use an asterisk (*) to indicate which are mandatory, and make as many fields as possible optional. Conversion rates decline incrementally for each additional field you force the prospect to fill out. The ease and convenience of accepting the offer can even be highlighted in the copy as a benefit. In a letter selling the Board Report, a newsletter for graphic designers, copywriter Sig Rosenblum makes a benefit out of the fact that the reply element is a BRC: Please complete the card enclosed and drop it in the mail today. It’s already addressed. And the postage is paid. 6. Minimizes the buyer’s risk and obligation. Do whatever you can to minimize sales pressure on the prospect. If you follow up leads by phone instead of with a field sales force, say in your copy “No salesperson will visit.” If you do not follow up leads by phone, say “No salesperson will call.” When offering anything free — a white paper, a webinar, even a brochure — say that it is free. Do not substitute the weaker “complimentary” when writing to a high-level business audience because you think “free” is not professional or will offend them. It won’t. However, if they are asking for a refund months after the guarantee expired, I tell them sorry but it’s too late. If they are reasonable or have been a regular customer, I may offer them a credit for a future purchase rather than a refund. Two More Tips for Strengthening Your Guarantees There are two other things to consider when creating your guarantee: Clarity. Make certain the terms and conditions of the guarantee are clearly stated and spelled out. Be careful about wording that the consumer can misinterpret. For instance, a performance-based guarantee — “If you do not earn extra money trading options with our program, return it for a refund” — sounds good but raises a potential concern. Namely, does it mean that if I DO make some extra money with the product, I can’t return it — even if I only made 10 bucks? Rewrite the guarantee so there is no condition or ambiguity stated or implied: “If you do not make extra money trading options with our program, or you are not 100 percent satisfied for any other reason — or for no reason — just return the program within 90 days for a full refund.” Make it stand out. The guarantee should be graphically emphasized within the promotion. Don’t bury it in body copy or put it in an asterisked footnote in 8-point type. Print the guarantee in 12-point type with a large, bold headline. Put a box or even a certificate-style border around it to make it stand out. Boost Orders Up to 21 Percent With an “Unfair Advantage” Offer E-books and other downloadable PDF information products present a unique problem as far as guarantees and refunds are concerned. With a hardcover or paperback book, if you want a refund you have to return the product. When you do, the seller has the book (which he can resell), you don’t, and you get your money back. But how do you return an e-book? The seller has the original PDF file, so they won’t want or need your copy. Even if you send it, how do they know you didn’t keep a copy on your hard drive? Some e-book sellers require customers requesting refunds to delete the PDF from their hard drive (and, I would suppose, throw away or rip up any printouts of the document). How do they know the buyer has complied? They don’t. Since there is no way to know whether a customer has deleted and destroyed their copy of my e-book, I don’t make them do it. In fact … I tell them they can keep it! Here — taken from the landing page for The Copywriter’s Toolkit — is my standard guarantee for the e-books and other downloadable PDF information products I sell online: _____________________________ Our 100% iron-clad guarantee of satisfaction I totally guarantee your satisfaction with this toolkit. If you aren’t convinced that The Copywriter’s Toolkit is the smartest investment you’ve made in your freelance copywriting business this year, just let me know within 90 days. I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. That way, you risk nothing. So what are you waiting for? To order The Copywriter’s Toolkit on a 90-day risk-free trial basis, just click here now: _____________________________ With such a policy, you might think that people would take advantage of me that and my refunds on e-books would be huge. Why should they pay for my e-books when they can essentially get them for free? The answer is that people are basically honest. Yes, a few do take advantage. But that small number is far outweighed by the increase in orders this strong guarantee generates. The proof: My e-book refund rate is a tiny fraction of 1 percent. And conversion rates increased once I added this copy to my sales pages. Internet marketer David Powers tested it, and found that telling buyers they could keep his e-book either way increased conversion rates and sales by 21 percent. My e-book offer allows the prospect to take unfair advantage of me: If they order the e-book and request a refund, they get it for free. Not only does my offer allow the prospect to take unfair advantage of me, my copy actively encourages them to do so: I’ll send you a prompt refund of your $39. And you can still keep the e-book with my compliments. We call this the “unfair advantage offer” — an offer where, if the prospect accepts it, he benefits unfairly … and the seller incurs loss. The reason to test an unfair advantage offer is its potential to boost response far in excess of the losses incurred from the few customers who exercise the guarantee. Another example: In 1999, one of my clients, a software publisher, was selling a tool that automatically recoded software to be Y2K compliant. When I suggested a 30-day money-back guarantee, the marketing manager balked. She was concerned that the buyers could use the tool to recode their software and then send it back, getting the benefit for free. “Let them,” I replied. In our marketing copy, we explicitly pointed out that they could use the tool during the 30-day trial to recode their systems. And that, after doing so, they could return the tool without paying for it, thereby “taking unfair advantage” of the software publisher. The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. _____________________________ Michael Masterson, copywriter, entrepreneur, and consultant for newsletter publishing giant, Agora, Inc., has a formula for creating compelling headlines. His Secret of the Four U’s © requires a headline to be unique, ultra-specific, useful (offering a benefit), and urgent. Without a sense of urgency, your promotion may not generate as many responses as you had hoped. And one of the most effective ways to get the prospect to “act now” is to build an element of urgency into your offer. Why It’s Important to Get Prospects to Act Now Instead of Later Your prospect is bombarded by direct mail, e-mails, telemarketing calls, radio commercials, TV spots, and other sales messages and offers. Which means that your best chance of getting her to respond to your offer is to give her sufficient motivation to do it right now, while the piece is still in her hands. There is an old saying among direct marketers: “A decision deferred is a decision not made.” If there is no “respond now” incentive, the prospect may think, “I’ll put this aside and get to it later.” Unfortunately, a directmail package is similar to the Sunday newspaper: If you don’t read it within 48 hours of getting it, chances are you never will. Too many other things surface to compete for your attention. How do you get the prospect to act now instead of later? The simplest mechanism is to put a time limit on your offer. This can either be (1) a specific date (“Offer expires March 15, 2009”) or (2) a generic time limit (“You must reply within 15 days to take advantage of this special free offer”). Both types of deadlines are effective. Which is better? A specific date is good if you have enough control over the timing of your promotion to ensure that delays in printing and mailing don’t make the date obsolete. For instance, you don’t want prospects to get a “Reply by April 15th” mailing on April 21st. If you do not have precise control over timing, or if you print your sales letters in large quantities and mail them regularly, a generic “Respond within the next 15 days” offer may be better. That way, no matter when the mailing arrives, it always works. How long should the time limit be? Which is best? 12 days, 20 days, 25 days, 30 days, two months, or something else? Obviously, the shorter the timeframe, the more pressure there is on the prospect to respond quickly. On the other hand, too short a timeframe may make the prospect feel rushed and uncomfortable. For direct mail, a 15- to 21-day deadline seems reasonable: short enough to motivate action, long enough to allow some breathing space. In e-mail marketing, deadline timeframes can be shorter. E-mails can say “Good this week only” or “Offer expires in 48 hours.” Sending one or two follow-up e-mails reminding prospects that the offer is about to expire as you approach the deadline can be very profitable in generating additional orders. On a landing page, you can have a clock or counter displaying, in real time, the days or hours remaining until the offer expires. Decades ago, Dennis R., a seller of mainframe utility software, used the standard 30-day free trial offer. Then he did a split-test of a 30-day free trial vs. a 60-day free trial. The 60-day offer outperformed the standard 30- day offer by 10 percent. “I concluded that the standard 30-day trial period was not sufficient for a busy IT professional to test our software,” said Dennis. “It would sit on the prospect’s desk for weeks. Then he would put off testing it for another week or two. And by that time, he felt he had to send the software back before he got billed for it. By extending the trial period from 30 days to 60 days, we gave the prospect sufficient time to install and test the software without fear of the free trial period expiring before he did so.” Apparently, 60 days was more than sufficient time for the software trial. When Dennis tested 90 days vs. 60 days, there was no further lift in response. Run all promotional copy past your attorney for vetting, especially time-limited offers. Once you state in your marketing that a certain offer expires on a certain date, you are generally not allowed to extend the offer beyond that date. Word Your Offer for Maximum Impact As I pointed out elsewhere in this book, the language you use to describe your offer can also affect response rates. In another mailing, Dennis tested the 60-day free trial vs. 60-day free use. This time, “free use” outperformed ”free trial” by 15 percent. Dennis concluded that the word “trial” had negative connotations for the IT tech who would be using the software. It meant screwing up batch files and coming in nights and weekends to do the testing. “But,” he said, “everyone wants to use a product — so who wouldn’t like ‘free use’?” For consumer mailings, the offer should require the recipient to reply within the next seven, 11, or 15 days. A common offer in direct mail is an additional “quick-response bonus” — usually a free report or other premium given as an incentive to reply within seven days. Offer expiration moves much faster in television infomercials. Merchandise is often offered on a payment plan — e.g., four easy payments of $19.95. The quick-response incentive is the elimination of one of the payments — the equivalent of a 25 percent discount — for viewers who call within a certain timeframe, usually 20 to 30 minutes. This time element can also be used online to establish a sense of urgency. To promote its annual copywriter’s conference, FastTrack to Copywriting Success Bootcamp & Job Fair, American Writers & Artists Inc. (AWAI) has used a digital display counting down to the expiration date for their early bird registration discount on their bootcamp home page. A variation of the specific timeframe offer is the limited number offer: “This offer is limited to the first 200 people who respond to this letter.” This tactic gets prospects’ attention because they have no idea how many pieces you mailed — and, therefore, are motivated to reply right away to ensure they are one of the first 200. Other variations? The limited offer is most effective when you can give a legitimate, credible reason why the offer is limited. Scarcity can be one such reason: The supply of what you are offering is limited, and, once it is gone, no more will be available. The late Bill Jayme had a clever scarcity line he used in direct-mail packages selling subscriptions to new magazines. It read: “Only so many copies of the premiere issue will be printed — no more.” That statement would be true no matter how many copies were printed. Nonetheless, it communicates a definite sense of limited supply. One computer company offered free prototyping of the prospect’s application. Because prototyping takes time and the company had a limited staff, it could handle only so many prototypes at one time. The sales letter made a point of this, saying, “We urge you to hurry. Based on response to previous mailings, we will get many requests for this free prototyping offer. If you are not one of the first to respond, you may well have to wait longer than we’d both like.” This worked because it was specific, credible, and true. If you don’t have a real reason why the offer is limited, you can invent one, and that can work. But when doing so, respect the intelligence of your prospects. For instance, one mailing I received many years ago told me I had to request a certain report right away because “We have printed only 1,000 copies and supplies are limited.” I suspected, of course, that if requests exceeded 1,000, the company would simply print more. So its act- now incentive lacked credibility for me. (The “limited quantity” offer is especially suspect when the premium can be downloaded as a PDF or MP3 file.) Another effective way to add a sense of urgency is to limit the total number of members, participants, or buyers. For a conference, seminar, or workshop, there really are only so many seats available — and no more. Tell prospects these limited seats are available on a first-come, first-served basis. In a promotion for a new $1,500 financial advisory service, a publisher told prospects that they had to act quickly because he could only take on 1,000 subscribers. Reason: With more than that, he could not make sure his subscribers got good execution on their trades. In his marketing copy he said, quite honestly: “If you apply after I have 1,000 members, I’ll have to return your thousand dollar check to you uncashed, as much as it pains me to do so.” Early-bird discounts are effective for events, and for pre-publication offers for directories, books, and other information products. For a weekend seminar costing $2,497, you might offer a $500 early bird discount, bringing the price to $1,997. For a book or directory selling for $100, even a $5 or $10 pre-publication discount is usually all you need to lift response rates. Give a Gift for Prompt Response A premium is a free gift the prospect gets for responding to your mailing. Does the premium have to relate to the product or service being sold? That depends on whether the purpose of the mailing is to generate leads or to make sales. Dick Benson, a successful consultant and entrepreneur, writes in his book Secrets of Successful Direct Mail (NTC) that it is not necessary for the premium to relate to the product being sold. The most important criteria for premium selection, according to Benson, are the perceived value and desirability of the premium. If the premium relates to the product, fine, but that’s of secondary importance. In lead generation, I agree that having a desirable premium is important, but I put more weight on trying to select a premium related to the product. Also, you have to be careful with premiums because many companies, especially defense contractors and subcontractors, have policies forbidding employees to accept gifts from vendors. In fact, a firm selling custom-imprinted business gifts by mail tested a straight 25 percent discount vs. a 25 percent discount combined with the offer of a free clock radio. Not only did the premium not increase response, it actually depressed it. Why? We can’t know for sure. Perhaps the buyers didn’t want to be perceived as accepting a gift or bribe for giving that vendor his company’s business. Whenever a mail order company attempts to bribe buyers with an expensive gift, some prospects might assume the merchant is inflating the price of their product to make up for the cost of the free gift — and they would rather pay less for the product and not get the gift. In business-to-business marketing, the corporate employee increasingly looks good to management by being a sharp buyer. That means getting the product at the lowest price possible. A larger discount might therefore work better than a free gift intended for personal use. If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, especially one working in a corporate setting, consider making it something related to the product and of value to the buyer’s company. For instance, a publisher selling highpriced technical journals and information databases on CD-ROM offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with the purchase of a group of its highpriced CD-ROM—based information products. The premium had high perceived value, was closely related to the product, and made the prospect look like a smart buyer. For lead generation, I think the best use of a premium is to offer something directly related to the product or service. My experience is that unrelated premiums of high value bring in large numbers of “freebie seekers” and other unqualified leads.
